thread: Capability is decentralizing while capital and policy centralize. Kimi K3 ships massive open weights and Terminal-Bench shows the top models in a near-tie — capability is spreading out. Yet ~$1T closed-lab rounds and the Blackwell export ban concentrate money and control. The two forces point opposite ways: if open models keep closing the gap, the moat moves from the model to the harness and distribution — which is why the MCP stateless shift matters more than any single model drop this week.

items.headline: MCP's 2026-07-28 spec moves the core from stateful to stateless request/response
items.why: Stateless lets you scale MCP servers horizontally behind a plain load balancer — no sticky sessions, no shared session store. Cost: it breaks cross-version compatibility, and Roots / Sampling / Logging + Dynamic Client Registration are now deprecated (12-month runway).
items.example: Today a stateful server needs sticky sessions — if your 2nd call lands on a different node than your 1st, the session context is gone and the call fails. Stateless means any node can answer any request.
items.connection: Ties to the thread: the 'harness > model' shift made concrete — as models converge, infrastructure like MCP is where differentiation moves.

items.headline: Kimi K3 — largest open-weight model yet (2.8T params, 1M context)
items.why: Open weights at this scale change build-vs-buy for agents, where per-call cost compounds fast. The tradeoff is raw capability vs. serving cost + latency.
items.example: An agent making 20 calls/task — a small model at ~1/10th cost wins for routing & tool steps; reserve a K3-class model only for the one hard reasoning step.
items.connection: Contrast: open weights this strong vs. the ~$1T closed-lab rounds (Investment) — capability decentralizing while capital centralizes.

items.headline: Paper: iStar — implicit step rewards for multi-turn agentic RL

ninety.method: Per-step implicit rewards so the agent gets credit on intermediate actions, not just the final outcome.
ninety.caveat: Benchmark-only; step-reward design is where the difficulty hides.

items.example: An agent finishes a 12-step task but fails at step 11 — with only a final reward it can't tell which step was good. Step rewards give signal along the way.

items.headline: Terminal-Bench 2.1: GPT-5.6 Sol (89.5%) edges Opus 5 (89.1%)
items.why: The top of the coding-agent frontier is now a near-tie, so the model is decreasingly the differentiator — the harness and eval design are.
items.example: A 0.4-pt model gap is smaller than the swing you get from a better retrieval/scaffold around the same model.
items.connection: Reinforces Kimi K3: if the best models are converging, the moat is the harness, not the model — the thread's core claim.

items.headline: OpenAI closes record $122B round ($852B post); Anthropic at $965B
items.why: The frontier-lab capital arms race sets the pricing umbrella everyone builds under — when top labs raise at ~$1T valuations, downstream API pricing and talent costs move with it.
items.connection: Contradiction with Kimi K3: money concentrates in closed labs even as open weights close the capability gap. Which force wins is the open question.

items.headline: Global VC hit record $510B in H1 2026; AI took ~80% of Q1 dollars
items.why: Capital is concentrating hard into AI, and valuations are priced for perfection — every non-AI startup competes for the remaining ~20% of dollars.

items.headline: House advances AI OVERWATCH Act; Blackwell export ban, H200 to case-by-case
items.why: Chip access is now a policy variable, not just a supply one — vendor and region choices can shift based on where you and your customers operate.
items.connection: Tension with Kimi K3: policy restricts hardware, but open weights let capability route around it — controls on chips don't fully control capability.
